MN202611_w2updenlu8.t:
A portrait of Daphne du Maurier sent to Fernande, her French finishing school tutor in August 1930

A set of photos of globally renowned 20th century author Daphne du Maurier has been shared by her family for the first time.

The photos show du Maurier in a series of family images, in settings including around Cornwall where she lived and did most of her writing - she died in 1989.

Her eldest grandson Paul de Zulueta found the pictures while researching a new book telling the personal story of his grandmother's artistic dynasty.

He said: "They were all tucked away in my mother's box. She said you might find this amusing - there's a box of photos here."

Du Maurier's novels which include Rebecca, Frenchman's Creek and Jamaica Inn continue to enthral readers, and often make the dark and brooding Cornish landscape central to the story.

Rebecca, written in 1938, has sold about 30 million copies worldwide and several of her novels have been made into TV shows and films.

Her grandson says writing about his ancestors and his famous grandmother has helped him understand her better.

One of the photos shows Paul's grandparents Daphne and Tommy outside Ferryside, around the time of their honeymoon in 1932

Daphne du Maurier and her husband Tommy in Fowey

De Zulueta was given access to du Maurier's private letters and photos, kept by his mother and his aunt.

His book Last Night I Dreamt tells of her connection to Ferryside, on the banks of the river Fowey in Cornwall, which has been a du Maurier family home for 100 years.

She first stayed there when she was 19, and it is where she wrote her first novel, The Loving Spirit.

Bodinnick, near Fowey, is also where she met her husband, Lt Gen Sir Frederick Browning, affectionately known as Tommy within the family.

When asked to pick two of the photos, De Zulueta referred to one showing the couple walking arm in arm not long after they married, and another of them in a boat.

"This is a particularly nice photograph of Daphne and Tommy in Fowey. Tommy my grandfather was wearing his brown leather jerkin.

"And of course this one is taken just outside of Ferryside in 1932. It must have been around the time of their honeymoon more or less, as they got married in July1932.

"So that photograph is particularly special I think."

Paul De Zulueta recently returned to Fowey to talk about the du Maurier family history at the town's literary festival

De Zueleta visited his grandmother in Fowey as a child every school holiday.

He remembers her being great fun, very mischievous and "someone with a great sense of humour, who filled a room with laughter", rather than the reclusive figure she is often described as.

He said: "She was extraordinarily happy here.

"And she said when she first came down to Cornwall 'this is the freedom that I have long sought.

"The freedom to write and the freedom to walk, the freedom to be by myself'."

She later moved to Menabilly, the house that was the inspiration for Manderley, the country estate in Rebecca.

Daphne and Tommy out together in Cornwall in early autumn 1933

Daphne (right), Tod (left, the family's housekeeper and governess) and the author's two children Flavia and Kits (standing) basking in the sun outside the east wing of Menabilly in 1952

Rediscovering his grandparents' relationship from the perspective of an adult has been a voyage of discovery for De Zulueta, who now believes his grandfather had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder after the war, for the rest of his life.

Browning's wartime service culminated in commanding airborne forces in the flawed Operation Market Garden, where thousands of troops parachuted into the Netherlands trying to seize key bridges from the Germans.

De Zulueta now recognises the stress his grandfather's absence would have had on the couple and the pressures of war meant "we need to judge the era softly".

He said: "They [Tommy and Daphne] had a very loving, deep relationship but it was unsettled at times.

"My grandmother was bisexual and she did also have an affair in 1942."

"I think Daphne regretted that affair, the family have never admitted to it, but I discovered a letter," he added.

Her grandson said reading her correspondence meant he had "got to like her a lot more".

"I always felt Daphne neglected him and therefore I was always in my grandfather's camp, but the more I read more about her life, I began to admire and respect her a great deal more.

"She was a great writer and how could she possibly be up in London trying to write books with my grandfather."

"She had to be in Cornwall because that was the ground-swell of her imagination," he added.

MN202611_1sbxpsqqm9k.t:
Ffion, Yugraj and Jessica say being ghosted has become a common part of applying for jobs

Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest challenge throughout the job-hunting process has been not getting feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

She says she has also been ghosted after interviews several times.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report , external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.

Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.

And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.

But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.

Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.

"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.

The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.

But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?

Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

Ellie says constructive feedback is always preferable to being ghosted

"If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is."

There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.

Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.

"Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on."

Bruno Fernandes has scored in each of his past two games for Manchester United

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says he has been offered a new contract by the club but feels it "is not the right time" for discussions about his future.

The 32-year-old midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season , though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.

He was left out of the side under previous manager Michael Carrick but says he has no issues at the club and has chosen to stay at Old Trafford despite offers elsewhere in recent seasons.

He told Sky Sports: , external "The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay.

"There's no negotiations ongoing, but I've seen people saying that 'he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years'. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.

"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here."

United chief executive Omar Berrada recently spoke about Fernandes' contract situation, saying: "It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private."

Fernandes has scored 75 Premier League goals since signing from Sporting in 2020 and last season set a record for the most assists in a Premier League season.

His form has tailed off this season in a poor start for the club as a whole.

United are 19th in the Premier League table going into Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge against rivals Liverpool on Sunday afternoon.

"We spoke about the contract at the end of last season," Fernandes said.

"We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

"The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games."

'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game

Fernandes was dropped for the Premier League defeat by Bournemouth last month after being critical of United's approach in their heavy defeat against Como in the Champions League.

But Fernandes says he did not fall out with Carrick, who was sacked on 12 November.

"The manager came to speak to me before the Bournemouth game, to say: 'Look, I'm not going to start you tomorrow. There's nothing to do with the words of Como, I know people will make it around that. I just want to tell you that we need to change something, I need to make a change, performances have not been great, so I just want you to know that there's nothing to do with that'," Fernandes said.

Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.

The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.

This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.

The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.

But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.

Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?

Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.

But the change seen in recent years has different roots.

There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.

The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24 , external .

In children aged under 16, it doubled from 6% to 12%.

That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.

The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.

Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment , external , since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35. Over half are under 45.

Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".

Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26% , external of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.

Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.

Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.

The pressure of social media and constant connectivity has been cited as a driver of mental distress

There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".

But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents , external .

Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".

Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.

Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey , external suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.

However, the 16 to 24 age group had the lowest score of any included, and around a quarter of young adults reported poor enough mental health to suggest a possible psychiatric disorder.

Young people have reported higher levels of anxiety and loneliness since lockdown

An independent review for the UK government by Prof Peter Fonagy last month said the problems faced by young people were real , with dramatically increasing cases of mental distress including depression and anxiety.

But Fonagy also warned of an "increasing risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis".

He said this was because "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier".

This was echoed by Alan Milburn, author of the UK government's review of support for young people in England and Wales.

He said that "in too many places, diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help", which has "created pressure on people to seek a diagnosis".

As an aside, it should be noted that while Milburn's review centred on employment prospects, benefit uptake does not always read across directly to this; Adult Disability Payment is not an "out of work" benefit like Jobseeker's Allowance.

The employment rate among disabled people in Scotland is more than 50%, and on the flip side studies have suggested , external that almost half of those not in education, employment or training are not claiming benefits either.

Alan Milburn's review could lead to a major shake-up of support in England and Wales

Milburn's review , external proposed sweeping changes to the youth support network in England and Wales, including faster access to mental health services and a complete replacement of Personal Independence Payments.

But in Scotland, "Pip" has already been replaced by Adult Disability Payment.

There was a very deliberate wave of publicity around the launch of the new benefit in 2022 - alongside the versions for children and pensioners - in a bid to increase uptake among people who might have been entitled to the likes of Pip, but never claimed.

With more money being spent on the Scottish system - it costs about £1bn a year over and above the block grant from Westminster - there is an easy narrative that it is inherently more generous.

A report last year concluded that it was more " significantly more compassionate " and "kinder in tone and approach".

However, it is worth noting that more than half of initial applications for ADP have been rejected, with 43% approved compared with 54% denied - broadly in line with the system in England and Wales.

There has been a steady increase in rejections since ADP was rolled out in 2022 - in the first few months only a quarter of applications were rejected, but over the past year it has been 67%.

Asked about this, Education Secretary Mairi McAllan said Social Security Scotland undertook a "very robust and close examination of all applications", and that people had to prove they were in need.

Last year also saw a record number of referrals rejected from NHS child mental health services , with ministers saying specialist services are only right for a small proportion of young people.

Mairi McAllan has said Scottish ministers will consider Milburn's report carefully

Even with an increase in rejections, the overall number of claims and the cost of the devolved social security system has been rising - and ADP alone makes up more than half of the total cost.

The last forecast from the SFC was for the social security bill to be £7.8bn in 2027-28 - within that, ADP accounts for £4.2bn, the pension-age disability payment £972m and child disability payment £659m.

By 2030-31, the cost is forecast to rise to £9.2bn - which has prompted questions from auditors and opposition parties alike about whether it is sustainable.

Ministers have repeatedly insisted that they view benefits as an investment in the people of Scotland.

But they have also said they will look carefully at Milburn's proposals.

A more generous system is not necessarily an easy choice, when it entails higher rates of income tax and cuts to other budgets.

There is also the possibility that changes down south could widen the existing £1bn funding gap, by cutting welfare spending at Westminster.

First Minister John Swinney has suggested that there are "potentially some significant financial implications that could be negative" for Holyrood.

But if money cut from benefits ends up being spent on education or local employment services - devolved issues - it would end up flowing back into the Scottish budget regardless.

Milburn's plan could apparently save about £200m a year by 2036-37, and while this would grow in subsequent years it should not represent a huge impact on devolved budgets.

And 10 years down the road the Scottish government's own public service reform plans, from the NHS to local councils, should have been worked through.

Who knows where we will be by then? The pace of change is relentless - in technology, in society, and in the health of the nation. The question is whether governments and policy can keep up.

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam

South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

Photos of the wedding on Saturday show the ceremony took place by a swimming pool with the pair standing under an arch covered in white flowers.

The singer's mother, Tish Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were in attendance, Entertainment Tonight reported.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, who donned a white dress for the wedding, confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.

'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton

Miley Cyrus confirms engagement to musician Maxx Morando

She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.

"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.

During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.

"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.

Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.

The singer, whose hits include Flowers and Party in the U.S.A, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.

Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".

Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

US rock musician Marilyn Manson has always strongly denied any allegations against him

A Brent councillor has joined calls to prevent Marilyn Manson performing at Wembley Stadium next year ahead of a trial the singer faces over sexual assault allegations.

Liberal Democrat Anton Georgiou has gathered more than 20,000 signatures on a petition urging the venue to take "a firm stand" against Manson, who is due to support Slipknot there in July.

Manson, whose real name is Brian Warner, is due to stand trial next November in a civil lawsuit brought by his former assistant Ashley Walters, who alleges sexual abuse. He denies the allegation.

Georgiou has written to the promoter Live Nation and Wembley Stadium urging the organisers to cancel the performance until a verdict is reached.

In a statement, Georgiou said: "If Mr Warner is convicted at the upcoming trial, this would reflect extremely badly on the stadium, risk untold reputational damage and send the wrong message to survivors of sexual abuse."

Slipknot fans hit back after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show

More than a dozen charities, who previously called for Manson to be removed from the line-up, have also signed the petition.

Manson has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct from several women, some of which have been dropped or dismissed. He denies all the allegations.

Previously, a Brent Council spokesperson said decisions about who performs at Wembley Stadium were "ultimately a matter for the venue and event organisers, rather than Brent Council, which has no direct control over commercial bookings".

"That does not diminish our commitment to tackling violence against women and girls, which has no place in Brent," they added.

"Our commitment to standing up for women and girls is unwavering, and we will continue to demonstrate that through our actions."

The BBC has approached Wembley Stadium and Manson's representatives for comment.

Ian Watson was in his first EFL managerial role at Rochdale

Rochdale have sacked head coach Ian Watson after only five months in charge of the League Two club.

The former South Shields boss replaced promotion-winning manager Jimmy McNulty in June after he joined Stockport but leaves the club just two points clear of the relegation zone.

Watson took South Shields to the National League North play-off final last season where they were beaten by Kidderminster Harriers before taking up his first Football League role at Spotland.

After returning to the EFL by beating Boreham Wood in last season's National League promotion final, Rochdale have won only four of their 16 League Two matches so far this season.

He departs following Saturday's 3-2 defeat by Northampton Town which was their fourth successive loss and left them 22nd in the table.

"We would like to thank Ian for his hard work and commitment during his time at the Crown Oil Arena and wish him every success in the future," said a club statement. , external

"The process to appoint a successor is already underway, and the club will give a further update in due course."

Rochdale are next in action at home to Barnet on Saturday, 28 November (15:00 GMT).

Othman Aland Koran at his poultry farm in Kamonyi district.

KIGALI – Othman Aland Koran was about 5 years old when his family left Iraq for Switzerland, beginning a childhood shaped by displacement, unfamiliar languages and the challenge of finding a place in societies far removed from the one they had left behind.

Coming from a Kurdish refugee family, he grew up among people from different parts of the world, many of whom had also been forced to leave their homes. The experience exposed him to different cultures early in life, shaping how he relates to people and sees the world.

Having lived in six countries, including Iraq, Syria, Bulgaria, Switzerland and Ethiopia, Koran is now building a new life in Rwanda, where he has established a poultry business in Kamonyi district.

Koran’s decision to settle in Rwanda followed years of international travel and a growing desire to find work that offered more than financial security. “I feel like I don’t belong to one country, I belong to anyone,” he said, describing a worldview shaped by years of moving between societies.

Although he had a good job in Switzerland and had managed to save money, Koran says he struggled to find meaning in a life centered on earning an income. “Clearly I was not happy. I had no meaning. Just making money wasn’t good for me,” he said.

With experience in food processing and manufacturing, an industry in which he has worked since the age of 16, he decided to venture into agriculture, beginning with poultry farming.

His project, which is about four months old, has a capacity of 5,000 broiler birds. It includes facilities for processing, solar power and ice production, allowing him to oversee the process from raising the birds to preparing fresh chicken for hotels and restaurants.

Koran wants to contribute to food security in East Africa by strengthening the supply of basic food products, with possible expansion into egg production and dairy farming.

He says agriculture offers an opportunity to put his professional experience to work in a sector he considers essential, even as farmers face difficulties making a sustainable living.

“Farmers are struggling a lot nowadays, and there may not be much money to be made. But with innovation and smart ideas, we can make agriculture more productive. Food is essential to all of us, and we need nutritious food,” he said.

Five months into his life in Rwanda, he describes his experience as unexpectedly positive, saying he had found business partners, people he could rely on and land for his project.

He sees Rwanda, particularly its position in East Africa, as a suitable base from which to pursue his ambitions while continuing to travel.

Koran was among the visitors at the second Rwanda Diplomatic Charity Bazaar held in Kigali on November 21, drawn by the opportunity to meet people from different backgrounds and experience cultures beyond his own.

His presence at the bazaar reflects another interest that has accompanied him throughout his travels which is bringing people from different backgrounds into closer contact.

Organized by the Intercultural Bridge Group CBC, the event brought together diplomatic missions, international communities, local artisans and businesses through exhibitions of traditional food, clothing, crafts and cultural performances.

Edison Niyontegereje, founder and chief executive of the group says the initiative is part of a broader effort to address the limited interaction that can exist between international communities and the people among whom they live.

Speaking at the event, he outlined intercultural education, cultural exchanges and intercultural dialogue as guiding programs through which the organization intends to pursue this objective.

The education program focuses particularly on helping international residents understand Rwandan society, while the exchange initiative seeks to create opportunities for Rwandans to experience other cultures and for foreign communities to learn about Rwanda.

“The organization also wants these relationships to generate opportunities for local entrepreneurs and creatives, including access to international networks and potential markets,” Niyontegereje pointed out.

Nigeria’s High Commissioner to Rwanda, Ambassador Ibrahim Zanna, said participation in the bazaar was also a way for diplomatic missions and their communities to appreciate the country hosting them.

He recalled that the inaugural edition introduced him to Rwandan artistic products, particularly traditional basket weaving, which he subsequently ordered. This year, he said had provided greater participation and interaction with Rwandan artisans and the Nigerian community.

“For us to show, to identify with anything that is being done by our host country is our own way of saying thank you for hosting us. More involvement even by Rwanda’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs could encourage more countries to take part,” he noted.

Alexander Sizov, Consul and diplomat at the Embassy of the Russian Federation in Kigali also highlighted the opportunity to learn about traditions beyond the political relationships that usually define diplomatic engagement.

“We should show our cultures and share what we bring to this country. Not only politics, but also traditions,” he said.

Such encounters are particularly important at a time when divisions between communities and nationalities remain a concern. With so many displaced people from different parts of the world, interaction is essential in building a more peaceful world.

Koran describes the warmth with which he has been received in Rwanda as one of the reasons he wants to establish a lasting base in the country. “Rwanda is the perfect spot to just have a base here which I can call home,” he said.

After a childhood spent learning how to adapt to unfamiliar places, Koran is now building something of his own in Rwanda, finding in agriculture not only a business opportunity but also a sense of purpose in the place he cherishes the most.

MN202611_14ea4fsxdee.t:
Alessio Dionisi was the fifth Italian manager hired by Watford under the ownership of the Pozzo family

Watford are looking for their sixth manager in 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following 18 games in charge.

The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

The decision to replace him comes after Saturday's crushing 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United at Bramall Lane.

Dionisi's dismissal caps an underwhelming start to the season, with the Hornets having won just four league games to leave them 21st in the table.

"We thank Alessio and his staff for his professionalism and their efforts," sporting director Luke Dowling told the club website. , external

"As I'm sure the supporters have seen, Alessio is a really good guy and we wish him the best for the future.

"The process has started for a replacement and we hope to be in a position to announce that shortly."

Dionisi was sacked by Serie B club Empoli in March after only five months in charge following a run of five wins in 22 matches.

His spell in charge of the Hornets was his first outside his homeland and started promisingly when his youthful side beat Southampton in their opening league game.

But they won only two of their next 12 in all competitions, and despite deservedly beating Charlton on 17 October, reverses at Wolves and Norwich followed, before four points from Dionisi's final three games in charge of the Hertfordshire side and his dismissal means further upheaval for the Hornets.

With more than a third of the league season complete, Watford are one place outside of the Championship relegation zone (table shown before Burnley face Blackburn on Sunday)

Since sacking Cleverley at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, the club has now been through four permanent head coaches, as well as interim boss Charlie Daniels' two-game spell in charge.

Of those four, only Gracia, in his second spell at Vicarage Road, took charge of more than 20 games.

On the morning of their final-day drubbing by Coventry last season, chief executive Scott Duxbury wrote a statement on the club website saying Watford had made mistakes, labelling their end to the campaign "unacceptable" and "truly disappointing in the extreme".

Mario Frick joined Aberdeen after leaving Luzern

If "heavy metal football" is what Aberdeen did, indeed, serve up at Kilmarnock on Saturday, Dons supporters will be eager to see more of this type of concert.

New head coach Mario Frick used the phrase in the build-up to his first game in charge and his team did not disappoint.

The 4-2 Rugby Park victory was bombastic, chaotic and end-to-end - just one of six goal-laden Scottish Premiership games on Saturday.

The four Aberdeen strikes - two from Kevin Nisbet and one each from Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall - showed Aberdeen's attackers at their best with fine finishing.

In the work in progress column, though, is defending, with the visitors lapsing badly for Killie goals scored by Greg Kiltie and Tyreece John-Jules.

All in all, it was an ideal start for former Luzern boss Frick.

Aberdeen's Frick starts with win in six-goal thriller at Kilmarnock

Watch new Aberdeen boss Frick score against Scotland

Frick was not a complete unknown to Scottish football when he was appointed during the international break - but the reference point was somewhat obscure.

Playing for Liechtenstein at Hampden in 2010, Frick gave the visitors a shock second-half lead.

The end of that game was reminiscent of the kind of heavy metal the head coach was talking about pre-match as Stephen McManus headed Scotland's winner after Kenny Miller's leveller.

Speaking after his Premiership bow, the former Luzern boss described himself as "very happy, very proud" of his new team.

"With only three training session, you can see so many attacking patterns in that first half, which was amazing," he told BBC Scotland.

"We struggled the first few minutes with some players that hadn't played in a long long time and the 1-0 lead helped. First half was very good, the second half, complicated, because Kilmarnock played very well. We were very lucky, but at the end, I think it is a deserved victory and we are very happy."

When asked if he was happy with the players trying to show his style, Frick replied: "Yes, for sure, after two training sessions, I saw a lot of it in the first half.

"It is a good start for us, but it is just the beginning."

Former Scotland midfielder Derek Ferguson took in the match at Rugby Park and was impressed with the visitors.

"As an attacking force, I thought they were good to watch," the former Rangers player said.

"They've got a big game on Tuesday night, against Rangers, so Rangers will need to be at their best, on their toes if they're going to get a result.

"It was the perfect result, obviously, for the manager coming in.

"There was more energy, more legs, more running power. They were winning a lot of the duels.

"It's something to build on, but they've got to work on that defence. They've got to be more solid if they're going to go forward."

Next up Ibrox and a season's third meeting with Rangers.

The two previous encounters, in the Premiership and League Cup semi-final, finished 1-0 to the Ibrox side, with the winning goal coming in the second half both times.

Meetings of Aberdeen and Rangers are typically just as fraught as the Rugby Park game on Saturday.

So, more heavy metal? It probably won't be smooth jazz.

We asked for your views following Aberdeen's 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.

Allan: One simple question. Why was [Ante] Palaversa nowhere to be seen under Stephen Robinson? I think the fans are due an explanation as to why both he and [Nicky] Devlin fell so far down the pecking order.

Brian: Much, much better is probably an understatement. Great entertainment and a big threat going forward and,as long as we score one more (at least) than the opposition then I will be happy. It is very noticeable that Jack Milne is much more steady when Nicky Devlin is playing. I am looking forward to the rest of this campaign.

Mike: Green shoots of recovery evident. Working as a unit from back to front has been a rarity at Aberdeen. If this is only after three training sessions, I am drooling at the mouth for what's to come. Stiff test on Tuesday, but the confidence must be there so nothing to fear.

Fred: Very positive start under the new manager. Good to see some direct attacking play but still a problem defending. An acid test coming against Rangers.

Abategetsi bavuze ko ibikorwa by'ubutabazi no kuzimya umuriro bikomeje ku bwato butwara imizigo bw'Uburusiya bwarashwe mu gitero cy'indege nto y'intambara itajyamo umupilote (izwi nka 'drone') mu burasirazuba bw'ikigobe cya Finland.

Ubwo bwato – bwitwa Sparta II – bwari burimo kujya ku butaka bw'Uburusiya bwo hanze y'ubuso busanzwe bw'Uburusiya, mu gace ka Kaliningrad kari mu nyanja ya Baltic, ubwo bwaraswaga mu gitondo cyo ku wa gatandatu, ubundi bukayobera mu mazi ya Finland.

Ingabo za Finland zavuze ko Ukraine ishobora kuba ari yo iri inyuma y'icyo gitero. Nta cyo Ukraine iratangaza.

Ku cyumweru, urwego rwa Finland rurinda imipaka rwavuze ko akazi kari gakomeje ko gutuma ubwo bwato butarohama ariko rwavuze ko nta byago ruzi ibyabaye byaba biteje ku ngendo zo mu nyanja zinyura mu bice bikikije aho hantu.

Kugeza ku cyumweru amazi yari akirimo gukoreshwa mu kuzimya umuriro kuri ubwo bwato, ndetse ibikoresho bya Finland, Estonia n'Uburusiya byari birimo gukoreshwa mu bikorwa by'ubutabazi.

Ashingiye ku makuru y'ibanze, Guverineri wa Kaliningrad Alexei Besprozvannykh yavuze ko 'drones' ebyiri zakoreshejwe muri icyo gitero, ndetse yavuze ko ibyabaye "nta nkeke" biteje ku bicyenerwa by'ibanze n'abatuye kuri ubwo butaka.

Minisitiri w'intebe wa Finland Petteri Orpo yagize ati: "Intambara irimo kugera hafi yacu cyane." Yongeyeho ati: "Ukraine ifite uburenganzira bwo kwirwanaho ku mushotoranyi."

Ubwo bwato bwa Sparta II bwafatiwe ibihano n'Amerika mu mwaka wa 2022 ndetse na Ukraine yabufatiye ibihano muri uyu mwaka wa 2026, kandi ni ubwa kompanyi yo mu Burusiya, nkuko bitangazwa na leta ya Ukraine na leta y'Amerika.

Ku rubuga rwayo rwo kuri murandasi (internet), iyo kompanyi ivuga ko yashinzwe mu rwego rwa minisiteri y'ingabo y'Uburusiya mu mwaka wa 2011 ndetse ko kuva mu mwaka wa 2015 ikora mu rwego rw'ubwubatsi bwo mu gisirikare.

Kaliningrad ni ubutaka bw'Uburusiya buri hanze y'ubuso busanzwe bw'icyo gihugu. Iri hagati ya Pologne na Lithuania.

Minisitiri w'ingabo wa Finland Antti Häkkänen yavuze ko urwego rushinzwe gucunga umutekano wo ku mipaka y'icyo gihugu ari rwo rurimo gukora iperereza kuri icyo gitero, kandi ko rurimo gukorana n'abandi bategetsi bireba.

Minisiteri y'ingabo ya Finland yavuze ko n'umuryango wo gutabarana w'Uburayi n'Amerika (OTAN/NATO) wabimenyeshejwe.

Inyanja ya Baltic yahindutse ahantu habera ibitero bya hato na hato mu ntambara y'Uburusiya na Ukraine, yatangiye ubwo Uburusiya bwagabaga igitero gisesuye kuri Ukraine mu mwaka wa 2022. Vuba aha Ukraine yakajije umurego mu bitero bigera mu ntera ndende igaba ku Burusiya birenga ahari imirongo y'imbere yo ku rugamba.

Muri uku kwezi, 'drone' ya Ukraine yarashe ubwato bw'intambara bw'Uburusiya mu kigobe cya Finland.
